prompt: Evaluate the extent to which technological innovation transformed the United States between 1865 and 1898.

documents.title: Bell's telephone patent
documents.source: U.S. Patent No. 174,465, granted to Alexander Graham Bell, March 7, 1876. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The patent's claim language, written by Bell himself to define what he had invented; shows how the invention was legally described.
documents.text: "The method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically, as herein described, by causing electrical undulations, similar in form to the vibrations of the air accompanying the said vocal or other sounds, substantially as set forth."

documents.title: Carnegie on the duty of wealth
documents.source: Andrew Carnegie, "Wealth," North American Review, June 1889. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A steel magnate's own argument for what great fortunes were for; shows how the men who made the new wealth justified it.
documents.text: "Individualism will continue, but the millionaire will be but a trustee for the poor; intrusted for a season with a great part of the increased wealth of the community, but administering it for the community far better than it could or would have done for itself."

documents.title: A Bessemer converter at work
documents.source: Nineteenth-century engraving of a Bessemer converter in operation. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A contemporary image of the new steelmaking process; shows the scale and heat of the work, and the workers beside the vessel.

documents.title: Miles of railroad in operation
documents.source: Emory R. Johnson, American Railway Transportation (1908), using Interstate Commerce Commission figures. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Official railroad figures across the period; shows the scale and the pace of the network's growth.

documents.title: United States steel production
documents.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), Table IX, Production of Steel. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Production figures across the period; shows how fast steel output grew once the Bessemer process spread.
documents.text:
| Year | Steel produced, thousands of long tons |
| 1870 | 69 |
| 1880 | 1,247 |
| 1890 | 4,277 |
| 1900 | 10,188 |

documents.title: The railroads adopt standard time
documents.source: Paraphrase of the General Time Convention's decision, October-November 1883, as reported by the Library of Congress. The facts are from the Library of Congress, "Today in History — November 18."
documents.sourcing: A paraphrase of the railroads' own decision; shows a private industry setting a standard the whole nation then followed.
documents.text: On November 18, 1883, at noon, the railroads of the United States and Canada set their clocks to a new system of four standard time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, and Pacific. Before that day, railroads had run on more than fifty different local times, and no two towns agreed on the hour. Within days, American cities adopted the railroad zones as their own local time.

documents.title: Lashing the stays of the Brooklyn Bridge
documents.source: Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, April 28, 1883. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A newspaper engraving of the bridge's construction; shows the dangerous work, high above the river, that steel made possible.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a thesis that makes a historically defensible claim about the extent to which technological innovation transformed the United States between 1865 and 1898, with a line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: A thesis that merely restates the prompt, or one that makes no claim about extent, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as post-Civil War industrialization, the growth of corporations, or the settlement of the West.
rubric.notEarned: A context that is only background on one document, or one set outside the period, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using the content of at least three documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least six documents to support the argument, with specific evidence from each.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least one piece of specific outside evidence, such as the transcontinental railroad, the telephone's spread, or farm mechanization, to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating document content without adding outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for explaining how at least one document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying a document's author without explaining why that matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a complex argument, such as showing that transformation was uneven, that new technology helped some Americans and hurt others, or that change and continuity ran together.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that ignores counter-evidence, or a complexity move stated without support, does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 technological innovation transformed the United States profoundly but unevenly, knitting the continent together, remaking cities and work, and concentrating wealth, while leaving many farmers, workers, and Native peoples worse off.
Context: The Civil War ended with a vast public domain, a railroad-building habit, and eastern industry hungry for grain, beef, and minerals.
Evidence: Documents 1, 4, and 6 show connection: Bell's patent, the railroad network growing from 35,085 to 193,346 miles, and standard time adopted by the railroads in 1883. Documents 3 and 5 show production: the Bessemer converter and steel output rising from 69 thousand to over 10 million tons. Document 7 shows the human cost and the new skyline: men lashing the Brooklyn Bridge's steel stays high above the river.
Outside evidence: the telephone reaching almost 50,000 users by 1880, the Pearl Street power station of 1882, farm machines doubling grain output while prices fell, and the transcontinental railroad completed in 1869.
Complexity: the same innovations that lowered prices and shrank distance also concentrated power, as Carnegie's own defense of great wealth in Document 2 shows, and the transformation reached cities and factories far faster than farms and reservations.
